newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Minorities, nationalists differ on Ukraine pact.
newsitem.headline: Minorities, nationalists differ on Ukraine pact.

text.p: Romania's ethnic minorities, including its 300,000-strong Ukrainian community, on Wednesday welcomed the imminent signature of a post-communist treaty with Ukraine, seen as vital for the country's NATO membership bid.
But nationalists denounced the pact and said it dashed any hope of recovering historic Romanian territories seized by the Soviet Union during World War Two.

"As Europe develops, borders will no longer mean very much. What matters is improving living standards and Romania has much to gain as Ukraine is a huge market," Varujan Pambuccian, an ethnic Armenian member of parliament told a news conference.
"Poland has signed a treaty with Ukraine despite also losing masses of territory precisely because it was in Poland's interests to reinforce Ukraine."
Presidents Emil Constantinescu and Leonid Kuchma are expected to sign the treaty early next month after years of negotiations often blocked by disputes over wartime history.
Romania has dropped its insistence that Ukraine atone for the seizure by the Kremlin of large chunks of territory under the Nazi-Soviet pact which carved up eastern Europe.
It has also abandoned a claim to a small Black Sea Island. Separate talks are to continue on setting maritime borders.

Romania won Western praise for signing a similar treaty with Hungary last year. Bucharest's leaders have been told they need the pact with Ukraine to keep alive their remote chances of winning quick entry to NATO.

Romanian nationalists said they would stage rallies to persuade Constantinescu to reject the treaty and launch fresh negotiations to take account of Romania's loss in 1940 of southern Bessarabia and northern Bucovina. Such rallies have drawn only a handful of activists in recent years.
"Signing this treaty is to commit an act of cowardice and treason," Nicolae Lupan, head of the Bessarabia and Bucovina organisation told a separate news conference.
"The country's leaders have no right to portray NATO membership as a prize in exchange for selling out the country."
Romania's chances of entering NATO in the "first wave" to be announced at an Alliance summit in July in Madrid remain dim despite backing from France, Italy and Canada.
The United States and Britain have given no such support and Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first to receive invitations.

Vichentie Nicolaiciuc, an ethnic Ukrainian member of parliament, praised the treaty and said talks had ended the practice of each side understating the size of minorities. He put the number of ethnic Romanians in Ukraine at about 400,000.
The accord, he said, would tackle the problem of education for minorities and access to media by cross-border monitoring. "It's a matter of if you don't give, I won't either," he said.
